FIG. 1. Lempel-Ziv complexity and the asymptotic behaviour. The four plots show the Lempel-Ziv complexity as a function of the string length N , compared with the same curve for the asymptotic behaviour N/ logN (Dashed black line). (a): even and (b): 2ssp correspond to finite-state automata defined in Appendix I. The first is the even process, which is controlled by a transition probability. Each colour corresponds to a different value of the transition probability. The second one (2ssp) is for the two-state symmetric process, which is also governed by a transition probability. (c): dna pertains to an experimental example, the DNA sequences of different mammals were used to factorise and estimate the complexity value. Finally, (d): random, stands for a random string. In all cases, the LZ-complexity is upper-bounded asymptotically by the asymptotic function as expected. What is interesting is that for large string size, the behaviour with the string length settles for an ansatz as described by equation (61). For short string lengths, all examples except the random case deviate from the asymptotic curve, which can be significant, as shown in the DNA data. The inset in each plot is the histogram, and the closer Normal curve of the distribution of factor lengths in the Lempel-Ziv factorisation.

FIG. 2. Convergence of the Lempel-Ziv entropy-density estimate with sequence length. Each row corresponds to one Hidden Markov Model process: (a) the two-state symmetric process (2SSP, top), (b) the even process (middle), and (c) RRXOR (bottom), swept across their full control-parameter range. Left column: the Lempel-Ziv estimate ĥ at four sequence lengths (N = 256; 5,000; 50,000; 500,000) overlaid on the true entropy density (red), each curve independently normalised between 0 and 1, (h − min)/(max−min), to compare shape convergence independently of each process’s own entropy range. Right column: root-mean-square error of the raw, un-normalised ĥ against the true entropy density, computed over the same parameter sweep, as a function of sequence length (log scale). In both columns, entropy density shows no qualitative convergence failure for any of the three sources, only a shrinking quantitative bias.

FIG. 3. Estimation of the effective measure complexity. Convergence of the effective measure complexity estimate across three Hidden Markov Model processes. Each row corresponds to one source: (a) the two-state symmetric process (2SSP, top), (b) the even process (middle), and (c) RRXOR (bottom). The control parameter τ is the transition probability of the two-state symmetric and even processes, and p is the probability of a 1 in the two free symbols of each RRXOR block (Appendix I, Fig. 9). Left column: the estimate Ê at four sequence lengths (N = 256; 5,000; 50,000; 500,000) overlaid on the true effective measure complexity (red), each curve independently min-max normalized, (E − min)/(max−min), to compare shape convergence on a common scale. Right column: root-mean-square error of the raw, un-normalized Ê against the true curve, over the same restricted range, as a function of sequence length. 2SSP converges cleanly to a low error floor by N = 50,000; the even process and RRXOR both improve steadily but substantially more slowly, and neither has reached a comparable floor even at N = 500,000, reflecting the longer block-size resolution their correlation structure demands relative to what Ĥℓ can reliably support at this sample size.

FIG. 4. Estimation of the effective measure complexity in the logistic map. The effective measure complexity estimated for the logistic map. (left) Ê as a function of the control parameter r; (right) The complexity-entropy map. Both plots can be compared to figures 1 and 2 of [13].

FIG. 5. Estimation of information distance by Lempel-Ziv complexity. Both plots show the information distance between the output string of the even process and a surrogate string for the whole range of transition probabilities. (a) The information distance between the string w and its negated string w̃(= w ⊗ 1, where ⊗ is the XOR logical operator). (b) The information distance between the string w and the reversed string w̆. The inset shows a detailed scale of the same plot. In both cases, the distance is nearly 1 for all transition probabilities, except for τ = 0, 1.

FIG. 7. Non-linear locally coupled oscillators. (a) Adler-type oscillators are coupled to their nearest neighbours as described by equation (81), forming a circular chain. (b) The entropy density map as a function of the control parameters ω and γ. Four regions are identified by the entropic magnitudes. The absorbing region has zero entropy density, while the chaotic region has a value near 1. For the wedge region, the entropy density is higher than the absorbing region but still lower than 1/2. Low values of h characterise the needle region. (c) Spatio-temporal map for γ = 1.206 and ω = 2.225 at the border between the needle and the chaotic region (edge of chaos boundary). Wave-like patterns can be identified. Time is on the horizontal scale, and the oscillator’s values are displayed vertically in consecutive order. (d) Detail of the spatio-temporal map. Point 1 is in the chaotic region, while point 5 is well within the needle region; all other points are at the border of the needle-chaotic regions. (e) The informational distance map for all points shown in (d) is split into even (above) and odd (below) oscillators. In the chaotic region (point 1), no distinguishable pattern is observed; by contrast, in the rest of the analysed points, characteristic patterns are seen in the maps. (f) The complexity-entropy map for each point shown in (d) in the chaotic region (point 1) shows that the odd and even oscillators are clearly segmented, with the even oscillators having higher ĥ values and lower Ê values. The segmentation becomes less clear for points on the edge of the chaos boundary, but there is still a clear grouping for each type of oscillator. At point 5, well within the needle region, the two sets of oscillators are again clearly segmented, with higher Ê values for both sets and smaller ĥ values.

FIG. 8. Electrocardiogram analysis.(a) ECG of a healthy subject (below) and a subject with atrial fibrillation (above). The AFIB patient has irregular heart rate behaviour. (b) The recurrence map of the (left) AFIB patient and the (right) healthy subject. The SR subject’s map shows clear, long diagonal lines parallel to the main diagonal, which are absent in the AFIB subject’s map. (c) The complexity-entropy map, derived from the estimation of the entropy density ĥ and the effective measure complexity Ê for each row of the recurrence matrix. SR and AFIB subjects are clearly segmented, with healthy subjects exhibiting higher Ê and lower ĥ. (d) Confusion matrix resulting from the training of a convolutional neural network fed with the vector of entropy density values. True negatives and true positives are above 82%.
